title: Payload edge fragmentation and backpressure sketch (May 2024)
content:
Goal:
Explore how tiny/fragmented streaming writes from the runtime interact with edge proxies (Envoy/nginx) and transport settings to produce tail latency and backpressure. Collect low-effort microbenchmarks and concrete heuristics we can try in the runtime and proxy layer.

Background / motivation:
- Recent customer reports (SERV-1234) of occasional 95th/99th token latency spikes when generating short payloads (1-4 tokens) with streaming enabled.
- Existing experiments focus on chunking size tradeoffs for long responses; fewer notes on the small-payload regime where fragmentation and write patterns dominate.
- Hypothesis: many small writes from the serving runtime cause packetization/tcp coalescing, proxies buffer and reframe streams, and TLS/TCP interactions amplify jitter.

Environment / testbed:
- Runtime: local dev cluster (4x A100-ish test VMs), runtime binary from branch streaming-optimizations-2024.
- Proxies: Envoy v1.28 (default config), nginx 1.21 (reverse-proxy config used for customer staging).
- Clients: python-requests + gRPC python client (async streaming) driving 1000 short-stream requests; also a simple Go client for precise timing.
- Tools: tcpdump, wireshark, perf, bpftrace, ss, strace, GO trace for client, /proc/net/tcp sampling.
- Network: 10G NICs, TLS on, colocated VMs to avoid cross-data-center noise.

Test cases (high level):
1) HTTP/1.1 chunked streaming, runtime writes small 128B frames every 10ms.
2) HTTP/2 (gRPC) streaming with 1-4 small responses (100B-1KB) per stream, inter-frame gaps at 5-20ms.
3) Mix: runtime does 1 small write then waits 50ms then more writes (to emulate token generation + KV cache lookups).
4) Proxy variations: Envoy default, Envoy with http/1.1 buffer limits lowered, nginx with proxy_buffering off/on.
5) TCP knobs: TCP_NODELAY on/off, socket write coalescing by enabling/disabling our batching layer.

Observations (notes, raw):
- With Envoy default and HTTP/1.1 chunked -> noticeable increase in P95: baseline runtime-only 12ms -> with Envoy ~ 28ms. P99 went from 18ms -> 110ms for certain small payload patterns.
- Packet captures show many 1-2 TCP segment packets carrying chunk headers followed by very small payloads; TLS records often end up as separate records for each chunk (overhead ~18-25 bytes per record).
- Envoy tends to coalesce multiple incoming chunks into a single downstream write in some configurations, but that coalescing is not deterministic and sometimes waits for a full buffer (configurable: http1/stream_idle_timeout-ish). The effect: occasional 50-150ms waiting window where Envoy accumulates bytes before forwarding.
- gRPC (h2) preserved better tail behavior when TCP_NODELAY=true on both client and backend; with Nagle enabled we saw batching-induced delays ~40ms.
- nginx with proxy_buffering on reduced downstream writes but added head-of-line delay when buffers full; turning buffering off pushed more pressure to backend sockets and reduced P99 on small-response tests.
- Kernel-level: TCP segmentation offload (TSO/GSO) on NIC can mask small write inefficiencies, but on TLS-offloaded proxies the coalescing behavior shifts and we observed TLS record flushes aligning with write syscalls.

Numeric summary (representative run, short-stream test, 1000 streams):
- No proxy, TCP_NODELAY on: P50 8ms, P95 14ms, P99 21ms
- Envoy default, TCP_NODELAY on: P50 12ms, P95 28ms, P99 110ms
- Envoy + reduce http1 buffer thresholds: P50 11ms, P95 20ms, P99 35ms
- nginx + proxy_buffering off: P50 10ms, P95 18ms, P99 40ms
- gRPC h2, TCP_NODELAY off: P50 15ms, P95 45ms, P99 150ms

Profile traces and interesting artifacts:
- bpftrace script on server write() syscalls shows bursts: multiple consecutive write syscalls separated by <1ms; when proxy downstream write is delayed the client-side read blocks for tens of ms (backpressure propagation).
- perf shows scheduling delays in Envoy worker threads at times of bursty ingress; those align with 100-200ms P99 events.
- strace on runtime: socket write returns EAGAIN occasionally when proxy is slow; our current retry/backoff is conservative and adds 20-50ms before reattempts which amplifies tail.

Root causes (working hypotheses):
- Fragmentation & small writes: the runtime emits many small writes for token-by-token streaming. Each write often maps to a TLS record and then a TCP segment unless coalesced. The overhead per record -> per-token latency.
- Proxy buffering/coalescing: proxies attempt to be efficient by coalescing but their heuristics are tuned for larger throughput patterns; when input is sporadic they can introduce wait windows that add jitter.
- Transport Nagle + TLS flush interactions: with Nagle enabled, small writes may be buffered until enough data or until a timer fires; TLS layers may also flush on record boundaries, creating multiple small TLS records.
- Scheduling/backpressure: when proxies are saturated (worker busy or buffers filling) backpressure reaches the runtime which then sees EAGAIN and our internal retry/backoff is too conservative.

Mitigations to try (ordered by low friction -> higher impact):
1) Runtime TCP knobs: ensure we set TCP_NODELAY on backend sockets by default for streaming routes. Quick wins in h2 and http1.1.
2) Adaptive coalescing inside runtime: instead of token-by-token write, coalesce small pieces for a 2-5ms window (configurable). Add an opt-in streaming_coalesce_millis. Must be conservative for high-throughput streams.
3) Proxy config recommendations: provide an internal doc with Envoy snippets (reduce http1/stream_idle_timeout, tune downstream_flush_on_body and buffer limits) and nginx: proxy_buffering off for low-latency streaming routes.
4) Backoff policy: change runtime EAGAIN handling to exponential with small jitter and shorter initial backoff (5ms). Capture metric for write-block events to surface in Console.
5) TLS record coalescing: investigate BoringSSL/OpenSSL socket write coalescing flags (SSL_MODE_NO_AUTO_CHAIN?) and whether the runtime can aggregate into larger records without breaking streaming semantics.
6) Client-side: recommend clients set TCP_NODELAY and prefer HTTP/2 when possible (fewer TLS record boundaries).

Open questions and follow-ups:
- How do these findings hold at scale across Dedicated clusters where network egress hits physical switches and more middleboxes? Repeat tests with multi-node, cross-rack setup.
- Is there a safe coalescing default that doesn't harm long-stream throughput? Need A/B with realistic workloads.
- Should we ship a profiling probe in runtime that counts small-write events and reports a "write-churn" metric to Console? That would help customers self-diagnose.
- Are there Envoy flags that deterministically disable the waiting heuristic? I couldn't find a single flag; need to look at connection manager code (Marcus to file follow-up PR).

Quick action items (owner -> task):
- Aisha: prototype streaming_coalesce_millis=3 patch in runtime; measure P99 on existing test harness (due 2024-06-05).
- Marcus: dig into Envoy code paths for http1 flush/coalesce heuristics and raise a small RFC/PR with suggested flags (due 2024-06-10).
- Sophia: add a lightweight write-churn metric to the tracing instrumentation and wire to dev Console dashboard (task SERV-1250).
- Ops: run a short replication in Dedicated staging (multi-node) to validate NIC-level effects and TSO interactions.

Notes / Loose thoughts (brainstormy):
- Could we wire a small shim in front of Envoy for low-latency routes that enforces immediate forwarding semantics? Dangerous but might be useful as a short-term knob.
- Consider documenting recommended "streaming profiles" customers can select (low-latency vs high-throughput) that flip TCP_NODELAY, proxy buffering, and runtime coalescing.
- For on-prem/private installs, shipping a validator that checks proxy configs (Envoy/nginx) for streaming route best-practices would avoid a class of customer surprises.

References / raw captures attached:
- tcpdump traces: /mnt/runs/2024-05-edge-frag/ (raw)
- sample pcap opened in candidate wireshark layout: file://pcaps/edge-frag-sample-1.pcap
- github PR with initial coalescing prototype: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/482
- ticket: SERV-1234 (customer report)

Bottom line summary (one-paragraph):
Small-payload streaming latency spikes are often a system-level interaction: tiny writes + TLS/TCP + proxy heuristics produce non-linear tail effects. There are several practical mitigations (TCP_NODELAY, small coalescing window, proxy config changes, and faster EAGAIN handling) that together can reduce P99 substantially with low risk. Next step: implement the runtime coalescing experiment + Envoy config tests and re-run the 1000-stream harness across a multi-node setup.
